alternative: Keep the GC for lifetime and use explicit resource management for owned resources: using/await using declarations with Symbol.dispose (TypeScript 5.2 / ES explicit resource management), close() plus try/finally on older targets, and typed addRef/release interfaces only for foreign counted objects at the boundary (COM, WASM/Node addons).
idiom_name: none - GC owns lifetime; using/Symbol.dispose at the resource edge
implementation_notes: TypeScript runs on the JavaScript GC, so an embedded count has nothing to free; what the type system adds is a contract for the two things that are real. Explicit resource management: an object implementing Disposable (a [Symbol.dispose] method) is released automatically by a using declaration at the end of its scope, in first-in-last-out order - TypeScript 5.2's release notes describe exactly this and point at the equivalent C#, Python and Java constructs. Foreign counted objects: a WASM/Node-addon or COM wrapper is typed as an interface with addRef()/release() so authors can see who owns a handle, even though the runtime never counts.
pitfalls: using requires a Disposable/Symbol.dispose object and a TS 5.2+/ES target (or downlevel helpers); plain objects are never disposed - there is no destructor to rely on.
FinalizationRegistry/WeakRef are typed but keep their documented non-determinism: cleanup callbacks are not guaranteed to run, so protocol state must not depend on them.

A typed { addRef(): void; release(): void } interface documents ownership but does not enforce it; every early return still needs the balancing release, and a double release of a native handle is fatal.
